title: Find duplicate elements in an array using HashSet (add each element to set; if `add()` returns false, it is a duplicate).
shortTitle: Find Duplicate Elements in an Array Using HashSet
keyPoints: HashSet.add() returns false when the element already exists, which instantly flags a duplicate.
Iterating once over the array and adding each element to a HashSet runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.
Collecting duplicates into a second Set prevents reporting the same duplicate more than once.
For counting how many times each element repeats, use a HashMap frequency counter instead.
Sorting the array first allows neighbour comparison with O(1) extra space but costs O(n log n) time and destroys order.
BigDecimal values must be compared with compareTo, not equals, when scale differences matter in banking amounts.

s1_definition.oneliner: Add each element to a HashSet; if add returns false, you have found a duplicate.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **HashSet** – a collection backed by a HashMap that stores only unique elements with average O(1) add, contains, and remove.
- **add() return value** – returns `true` if the element was new and `false` if it already existed, which is the core duplicate-detection trick.
- **Linear scan** – one pass over the array with a HashSet gives O(n) time and O(n) extra space.
- **Duplicate collection** – storing found duplicates in a second `Set` prevents reporting the same value more than once if it appears three or more times.
- **Alternative** – sorting the array first lets you compare neighbours with no extra set, at the cost of O(n log n) time and loss of original order.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a guard maintains a guest list of account numbers that have already entered the vault today. As each person arrives, the guard tries to write their account number on the list. If the number is brand new, it gets written and they pass. If the guard finds the number is already on the list, that is a duplicate entry and it is flagged immediately without scanning the whole list.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicate elements in an array, the standard approach is a single-pass HashSet scan. You iterate once over the array and try to add each element to the set. The `add` method returns `true` if the element was new and `false` if it was already present, so a `false` return instantly tells you that you have found a duplicate. That single boolean is the elegant core of the technique, and the whole algorithm runs in O(n) time with O(n) space.

A detail that matters is collecting the duplicates into a second Set rather than a List. If an element appears three or more times, a List would record it multiple times, whereas a Set guarantees each duplicate is reported exactly once. When you also need how many times each value repeated, switch to a HashMap frequency counter and keep the keys whose count exceeds one.

In the settlement service at the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in a de-duplication gate. A nightly batch of processed transaction IDs arrives from a payment partner, and because of retries the same ID sometimes appears twice. Posting a duplicate would double-charge a customer like Priya, so before posting, the service scans the batch with a HashSet, and if any duplicate is detected, it blocks the batch and alerts the operations team.

The senior-level angle is the space-time tradeoff. The HashSet approach is fast and preserves input order but uses extra memory proportional to the distinct elements. Sorting the array first allows neighbour comparison with zero extra space, but it costs O(n log n) time and destroys the original order. For massive streaming data, a Bloom filter trades a tiny false-positive rate for far less memory. For a normal batch, the HashSet method is the clean, correct, production choice.

Remember one sentence: add each element to a HashSet, and when `add()` returns false, you have found a duplicate.
